blocks.content: Understanding exactly what happens when you run docker build demystifies a lot of behavior that otherwise looks like magic, especially around caching and layer creation.
1. The Dockerfile Is Sent to the Daemon
blocks.text: 1. The Dockerfile Is Sent to the Daemon

blocks.content: Running docker build does not execute instructions on your local client, the client packages up the Dockerfile and the build context and sends them to the daemon, which does the actual building, exactly the same client-daemon split covered in the Architecture module.

blocks.alt: The daemon does the actual building work

blocks.content: The daemon works through the Dockerfile one instruction at a time, and (for most instruction types) produces a new layer for each one, stacked on top of the last, exactly as covered in the Image Layers topic.

blocks.alt: One instruction at a time, one layer at a time

blocks.content: 3. Every Step Checks the Cache First
blocks.text: 3. Every Step Checks the Cache First

blocks.content: Before actually executing an instruction, the daemon checks whether it already has a cached layer for that exact instruction, in that exact position, with unchanged input. If so, it reuses the cached layer instead of doing the work again, this is the mechanism behind the Image Caching topic from the previous module.

blocks.alt: A cache check happens before every single instruction

blocks.content:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
# Sending build context to Docker daemon  4.2MB
# Step 1/6 : FROM node:18
#  ---> Using cache
# Step 2/6 : WORKDIR /app
#  ---> Using cache
# ...

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A build sends your Dockerfile and context to the daemon, which executes instructions in order, one layer per instruction.
Every instruction checks the build cache first, "Using cache" in the output means that layer was reused, not rebuilt.
